conclusion: Confluence is usually read as order-independence of reduction, while flatness is usually read as path-independence of transport. This paper argues that their local cores coincide once rewriting is equipped with its missing two-dimensional cells. The relevant object is not the bare reduction graph but a reduction 2-complex whose 0 -cells are states, whose 1 -cells are one-step rewrites, and whose generating 2 -cells are local peaks or, in structured rewriting settings, reachable critical pairs. In that setting, elementary flatness is exactly local confluence. We prove this core equivalence and record the supporting fact that confluence plus normalization yields a unique normal form from a chosen start state. We then show computationally that the corrected local/global picture survives exhaustive finite-ARS stress tests in the terminating regime, curated string-rewriting examples, and a curated left-linear term-rewriting bridge with genuine nonroot overlap. These experiments also show that bare graph-flatness surrogates fail, while reachable critical-pair defects align with the observed local obstruction layer. Finally, explicit before/after examples show that completion can be read as holonomy elimination: the local generator persists while its defect disappears. The full finite terminating left-linear TRS theorem package remains to be written in full generality, but the correct object, local generators, and evidence boundary are now fixed.

conclusion: We use the Six Birds vocabulary of closure mechanics introduced in . The six primitives are: P1: operator rewrite, P2: constraints or feasibility gating, P3: route mismatch / holonomy, P4: staging, P5: packaging, P6: accounting / audit. The present paper is primarily a P3 paper. Its central object is local route mismatch in rewriting systems. P5 and P6 play supporting roles by packaging the rewriting layers and by keeping the defect structure explicit in machine-readable artifacts and audits. The mathematical development below is otherwise self-contained.
expanded_source_wording_tex:
\label{rem:six-birds-primitives}
We use the Six Birds vocabulary of closure mechanics introduced in \cite{Tsiokos2026SixBirdsFoundations}. The six primitives are:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{P1}: operator rewrite,
    \item \textbf{P2}: constraints or feasibility gating,
    \item \textbf{P3}: route mismatch / holonomy,
    \item \textbf{P4}: staging,
    \item \textbf{P5}: packaging,
    \item \textbf{P6}: accounting / audit.
\end{enumerate}
The present paper is primarily a \textbf{P3} paper. Its central object is local route mismatch in rewriting systems. \textbf{P5} and \textbf{P6} play supporting roles by packaging the rewriting layers and by keeping the defect structure explicit in machine-readable artifacts and audits. The mathematical development below is otherwise self-contained.

conclusion: For the purposes of this paper, a reduction 2-complex associated to a rewriting system R consists of the following data. A set of 0 -cells, namely the states, words, or terms under consideration. A set of directed 1 -cells, namely the one-step rewrites x → y . A set of generating 2 -cells, each attached to a local two-route branching pattern with common source. In the finite-ARS setting these are local peaks. In the string and term-rewriting settings used in this paper, these are reachable critical pairs relative to the chosen start states and exploration bounds.

conclusion: Let sigma be a generating 2 -cell with source x and one-step branches to y_ and y_r . Its boundary data consist of x → y_ and x → y_r. A filler for sigma is a common descendant w together with directed paths y_ →^* w and y_r →^* w. When such a filler exists, we call w a join witness for sigma .
expanded_source_wording_tex:
\label{def:boundary-filler-data}
Let $\sigma$ be a generating $2$-cell with source $x$ and one-step branches to $y_\ell$ and $y_r$. Its boundary data consist of
\[
x \to y_\ell
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
x \to y_r.
\]
A \emph{filler} for $\sigma$ is a common descendant $w$ together with directed paths
\[
y_\ell \to^* w
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y_r \to^* w.
\]
When such a filler exists, we call $w$ a \emph{join witness} for $\sigma$.

conclusion: An elementary peak is a triple (a,b,c) such that a → b, a → c, b ≠ c. The rewriting system (X,→) is elementarily flat if every elementary peak is joinable.
expanded_source_wording_tex:
\label{def:elementary-peak-flatness}
An \emph{elementary peak} is a triple $(a,b,c)$ such that
\[
a \to b,
\qquad
a \to c,
\qquad
b \neq c.
\]
The rewriting system $(X,\to)$ is \emph{elementarily flat} if every elementary peak is joinable.

It does not yet identify which local branchings generate the relevant $2$-cells in a given rewriting formalism; that is the role of critical pairs in \Cref{sec:critical-pairs-curvature}. Nor does it by itself supply a local-to-global theorem such as Newman-style termination plus local confluence \cite{Huet1980,BaaderNipkow1998,DershowitzJouannaud1990,Terese2003}. Its point is narrower and more precise: once the correct elementary branchings have been identified, ``flatness'' at that level is exactly local confluence.

expanded_source_wording_tex:
\label{def:confluence-normalization}
The rewriting system $(X,\to)$ is \emph{confluent} if for all $a,b,c \in X$,
\[
a \to^* b
\quad\text{and}\quad
a \to^* c
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
b \text{ and } c \text{ are joinable.}
\]
It is \emph{normalizing} if for every $a \in X$ there exists some normal form $n$ such that
\[
a \to^* n.
\]

\begin{itemize}
    \item finite abstract rewriting systems,
    \item reflexive-transitive reachability,
    \item joinability,
    \item normal forms,
    \item local confluence,
    \item elementary peaks,
    \item elementary flatness.
\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}
    \item confluence,
    \item normalization,
    \item uniqueness of normal form from a chosen start state,
    \item existence and uniqueness of normal form under confluence and normalization.
\end{itemize}
